# Run a talker on an emulated board

<!-- type: tutorial · level: 1 -->

**Needs first:** [Install](../start/install.md)

<!-- BEGIN GENERATED by scripts/gen-board-support.py: chapter status -->
> **Status:** this chapter runs on [`nros-board-mps2-an385`](../reference/boards/mps2-an385.md): Verified in emulator (daily). From the board support registry; [Board Support Levels](../reference/board-support-levels.md) explains the words.
<!-- END GENERATED chapter status -->

By the end of this chapter, an Arm Cortex-M3 board emulated by QEMU is
printing `Publishing: 'Hello World: 1'`, `'Hello World: 2'` and onward, once a
second, and `ros2 topic echo` on your machine prints the same messages as they
arrive. You write no code and edit no configuration to get there: you
provision the board, scaffold a project, and run it.

This chapter starts the one project the whole Tutorial grows. Each later
chapter adds to the workspace you create here, so keep it.

## What you need

- A Linux host with the [install](../start/install.md) done, so `nros` is on
  your `PATH`.
- ROS 2 Humble with its zenoh middleware, `ros-humble-rmw-zenoh-cpp`. ROS 2
  gives you the router the board talks to, the `ros2` command that shows its
  messages, and the message definitions the build generates the talker's code
  from. If you have no ROS 2 install, the container in
  [Install options](../guide/build/install-options.md#ros-2-and-the-zenoh-router)
  has one.

You need no board, no cable and no root access. The emulated board talks to
your machine over its serial port, the way a real board's first program does.
Its network comes later, in the board's own page,
[Bare-metal Cortex-M3](../guide/platforms/bare-metal.md). WiFi is deferred:
no chapter uses it yet.

The board is Arm's MPS2-AN385, which QEMU models closely. No one buys one: it
is the board this book teaches nano-ros on, because it costs nothing and
behaves like a real microcontroller. "Bare-metal" means the talker runs with no
operating system under it, as one loop on the processor.

## Provision the board

```bash probe=30 track=installed variant=qemu
nros setup mps2-an385-baremetal --rmw zenoh
```

This fetches the Arm cross-compiler, a QEMU that emulates the MPS2-AN385, and
the Rust target for the Cortex-M3, into a shared store under `~/.nros`.
Nothing is installed system-wide, and a second project for the same board
reuses what this step fetched. Running it again is quick: it checks what is
there and fetches only what is missing.

`--rmw zenoh` names the middleware the talker uses to reach ROS 2. nano-ros
offers three, and zenoh is the one that runs over a serial port on this board,
so it is the one this Tutorial starts with. `nros setup` fetches only what that
middleware needs on this board. Chapter 4 compares the three and shows what
each one needs beside your program.

## Scaffold the project

Pick the language you will write the project in. Every later chapter shows
its code in the same three languages, and the project keeps the language you
pick here.

<!-- tabs -->

#### Rust

```bash probe=40 track=installed variant=qemu
nros new sensor_ws --board mps2-an385-baremetal --template talker --lang rust
cd sensor_ws
```

#### C

```bash probe=40 track=installed variant=qemu
nros new sensor_ws --board mps2-an385-baremetal --template talker --lang c
cd sensor_ws
```

#### C++

```bash probe=40 track=installed variant=qemu
nros new sensor_ws --board mps2-an385-baremetal --template talker --lang cpp
cd sensor_ws
```

<!-- /tabs -->

`nros new` prints what it wrote and the command that runs it. The workspace
holds two packages:

```text
sensor_ws/
└── src/
    ├── sensor_node/            # your node: package.xml, its build file, its source
    └── sensor_node_bringup/    # which board it runs on; you don't need to open it yet
```

`sensor_node` is the code: a talker that publishes `std_msgs/String` on
`/chatter` once a second. Its build file is a `Cargo.toml` in Rust and a
`CMakeLists.txt` in C and C++. `sensor_node_bringup` says what that code runs
on. The scaffold filled it in, and this chapter never needs you to open it.
The next chapter opens both.

The same shape, kept for reading beside this chapter, is
[`examples/mps2-an385-baremetal/rust/talker/`](https://github.com/NEWSLabNTU/nano-ros/tree/main/examples/mps2-an385-baremetal/rust/talker)
in the nano-ros repository.

## Run it

Source ROS 2 first, then run. ROS 2 provides the router the board talks to,
and its message definitions are what `nros run` generates the talker's
`std_msgs` code from. This first run records the ROS 2 prefix in the
workspace, so a later build of it needs no sourced shell. The router still
does, because it is a ROS 2 program.

```bash probe=50 probe-run=1500 track=installed variant=qemu
source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
nros run sensor_node --expect 'Publishing:'
```

```text probe-expect=50 variant=qemu
Publishing: 'Hello World: 1'
nros run: matched after
```

The first run compiles nano-ros for the Cortex-M3 and takes a few minutes;
later runs rebuild only what changed and take seconds. After the build, the
end of the output looks like this (a run on a Linux host with the build tree
under `/home/you`, trimmed):

```text
nros run: starting the zenoh router on serial//dev/pts/42#baudrate=115200

========================================
  nros QEMU Platform
========================================

Initializing CMSDK UART serial...
  Base: 0x40004000
  Baud: 115200
Serial ready.

Application setup complete — entering spin loop.
[INFO] sensor_node: [    1.024551] Publishing: 'Hello World: 1'
nros run: matched after 3.6 s: [INFO] sensor_node: [    1.024551] Publishing: 'Hello World: 1'
```

Everything after the router line is the board's console: the banner its
startup code prints, the serial port coming up, then the talker. The number in
brackets is the board's own clock, in seconds since it booted. A C or C++
talker prints its `Publishing:` line without the `[INFO]` prefix.

With `--expect`, `nros run` stops everything and exits 0 the moment the
console prints a line containing that text. It exits 1 if the board stops
first, and `--timeout <secs>` bounds the wait. That makes it a one-line check
that the whole path works, which is how the rest of this Tutorial checks each
chapter's result.

Without `--expect`, it keeps streaming until you press Ctrl-C, which stops
QEMU and the router together. Start it that way in one terminal (source ROS 2
first if it is a new terminal, because the router comes from ROS 2):

```bash probe=55 probe-run=300 probe-keep track=installed variant=qemu
source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
nros run sensor_node
```

```text probe-expect=55 variant=qemu
Publishing: 'Hello World: 2'
```

## See it in ROS 2

Leave `nros run` going. In a second terminal:

```bash probe=60 probe-run=120 track=installed variant=qemu
source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
export RMW_IMPLEMENTATION=rmw_zenoh_cpp
ros2 topic echo /chatter std_msgs/msg/String --qos-reliability best_effort
```

```text probe-expect=60 variant=qemu
data: 'Hello World:
```

`ros2 topic echo` prints one `data:` line per message, followed by `---`:

```text
data: 'Hello World: 7'
---
data: 'Hello World: 8'
---
```

The command asks for best-effort delivery, which receives from a publisher
of either kind, so it works whatever QoS a publisher offers. This talker's
publisher happens to be reliable, as `ros2 topic info -v /chatter` shows, and
a plain `ros2 topic echo /chatter` hears it too. Chapter 10 explains the QoS
rules that decide what a subscriber hears, and where nano-ros differs from
ROS 2 on the wire.

Press Ctrl-C in both terminals when you have seen enough.

## Change it

Open the talker's source, change the `"Hello World"` text, and run
`nros run sensor_node` again. It rebuilds what changed and boots the new
program.

<!-- tabs -->

#### Rust

The text is in `src/sensor_node/src/lib.rs`, in the line that formats the
message:

```rust
let _ = write!(msg.data, "Hello World: {}", *state);
```

#### C

The text is in `src/sensor_node/src/Talker.c`, in `on_tick`:

```c
snprintf(self->msg.data.data, self->msg.data.capacity, "Hello World: %d", (int)self->count);
```

#### C++

The text is in `src/sensor_node/src/Talker.cpp`, in `on_tick`:

```cpp
std::snprintf(payload, sizeof(payload), "Hello World: %d", count_);
```

<!-- /tabs -->

Keep the message under 64 bytes: the talker formats it into a fixed buffer,
because each message is built in a buffer whose size is fixed when the
program is built.

## What just happened

You ran a ROS 2 talker on a microcontroller without writing any of the
program around it. Four things worked together, and each later chapter
changes one of them:

1. **The build.** `nros run` compiled your talker and nano-ros for the
   Cortex-M3, a 32-bit Arm core with no memory protection and no operating
   system. The program it built contains the talker, the code that starts the
   board, and the zenoh client that carries messages.
2. **The board.** QEMU booted that program as the MPS2-AN385 would. The
   board's first serial port, UART 0, is connected to a terminal device on
   your host (`/dev/pts/42` in the output above). The board has no network in
   this chapter, so that serial port carries every message. What the program
   prints reaches your terminal separately, through QEMU itself, which is why
   the console and the messages do not mix.
3. **The router.** `nros run` started ROS 2's zenoh router, `rmw_zenohd`, on
   that terminal device. The router speaks zenoh over the serial line to the
   board, and over TCP to every ROS 2 program on your machine. nano-ros ships
   no router of its own: the one ROS 2 already uses is the one the board
   reaches.
4. **ROS 2.** `ros2 topic echo` with `RMW_IMPLEMENTATION=rmw_zenoh_cpp`
   connected to the same router and subscribed to `/chatter`. To ROS 2, the
   board is one more node on the graph.

The talker itself is the same kind of node you would write for ROS 2: a
publisher, a timer, and a callback that publishes on every tick. What differs
is around it. The program is built for one board, its messages are built in
buffers of fixed size, and its memory is fixed when it is built. The next chapter opens the
two packages and shows where each of those facts is stated.

## No QEMU, no router: run it on this machine

The same flow runs on your Linux host, with Cyclone DDS, which needs no
router. Only the board in the scaffold line changes; the node code has the
same shape, and so does every command after it.
[Get started on the Linux host](../starters/linux-host.md) takes it step by
step. Chapter 9 adds the host to this project as its second target.

## If nothing appears

- **`nros run` stops at once and names `AMENT_PREFIX_PATH`:** this
  shell has not sourced ROS 2, and no earlier build of the workspace
  recorded it. Run `source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash` and run again.
- **`nros run` says the router exited (code 127):** the router is a ROS 2
  program, and this shell has not sourced ROS 2, so it could not start.
  Source ROS 2 in that shell and run again.
- **`nros run` stops at once and names the router:** it could not find
  the zenoh router. Install `ros-humble-rmw-zenoh-cpp` if it is missing, or
  point `NROS_RMW_ZENOHD` at an `rmw_zenohd` binary.
- **No `Publishing:` line within a minute of boot:** the router started
  but the board did not reach it. `nros run` names the router's log when
  it stops.
- **`ros2 topic echo` prints nothing:** check the `--qos-reliability
  best_effort` flag and the `RMW_IMPLEMENTATION` line.

[Troubleshooting index](../reference/troubleshooting-index.md) has the rest.

The chapter follows [RFC-0116](https://github.com/NEWSLabNTU/nano-ros/blob/main/docs/design/0116-adoption-purposes-and-front-doors.md)
D5 and D6, [RFC-0121](https://github.com/NEWSLabNTU/nano-ros/blob/main/docs/design/0121-workspace-first-project-layout.md)
D4 and D5, and [RFC-0124](https://github.com/NEWSLabNTU/nano-ros/blob/main/docs/design/0124-book-user-guide-organization.md)
D3: one Tutorial project on a Verified board. Its pointer to the copy-out
talker follows [RFC-0122](https://github.com/NEWSLabNTU/nano-ros/blob/main/docs/design/0122-behaviour-bringups-road-witnesses-cadence-backed-ci.md)
D3.
